title: Anyone ever seen or been in a re-imagined version of one his plays? #...
transcript: Did you know there's a living playwright who not only put all of his scripts online for free, but also allows you to adapt them however you want? This is Charles Mee. And in addition to being a prolific playwright, he's largely known for what he calls the (re)making project. Part of the idea is that a lot of his plays were inspired by or adapted *from other classical texts. And so he wants other people to treat his plays the way he treated those classical plays. So he literally put them all on his website for free. But there's a catch. He says, “use them freely as a resource for your own work.” “Don't just make some cuts or rewrite a few passages,” “but pillage the plays” “as I have pillaged the structures and contents of the plays of Euripides” etc. “And then please put your own name on the work that results.” But if you wanna do the plays pretty much as he wrote them, he still request that you license them through official channels the way you would for any other play. I was actually in a production of one of his plays, Big Love, when I was in college, and they didn't actually change it around that much. We pretty much did it as he wrote it. But the production they did at my high school, which I wasn't in, but I saw it, they didn't have enough roles for all the actors, so they just Like, inserted some more roles. And it was seemingly in the same spirit that Charles Mee decided to premiere his newest play, Prelude, in a public plaza in Brooklyn for free. It just played for three performances only at BAM's Next Wave Festival. It was directed by Anne Bogart. It had original songs by the Lazours and really awesome costumes by Machine Dazzle. It was essentially a series of conversations and arguments between between an old couple and a young couple, observed by the waiter of a cafe where they both sit. And then each of the five actors had a kind of counterpart wearing one of these really zany costumes that kind of reflected something about the characters inner life. And they would sometimes mirror their movements, sometimes compliment them, or even intermingle with each other. And at the end of the performance, the playwright himself gave a short speech talking about how he likes plays that are not too neat, too finished, or too presentable, but that have jagged edges. That this reflected a sense of chaos in his own life and in society.
classificationReason: Educational explainer about playwright Charles Mee and his (re)making project/open licensing model. No specific listed production is reviewed or discussed.
